prompt: Write a restrained but distinctive scene set in a small shoe-repair shop on its last evening. Two coworkers disagree about what to leave behind. Let practical actions change their understanding of one another. Avoid a surprise letter, deathbed revelation, or concluding moral. Use an appropriate voice of your choosing; quietness is not itself a defect.

commitments.text: Only Sana and Tomas are physically present in the shop.
The shop closes because its lease ends, not because either person has died.

prompt: Write a scene in which Ivo confidently believes the rain began after noon while the reader knows it began at ten. His mistaken belief should affect a practical choice without making him foolish. Maintain the difference between world facts, his belief, and reader knowledge. By the end he has not learned when the rain actually began. Do not explicitly explain the theme.

world.text: Rain began at ten in the morning.
Ivo believes the rain began after noon.

reader.text: The reader already knows rain began at ten.

commitments.text: Ivo does not discover the true start time during this scene.

prompt: Write one continuous scene at a lost-property counter. The disputed object is an ordinary umbrella. Make the encounter surprising through the characters' specific motives and choices, while keeping the object ordinary. You may use humor, reserve, tension, or another coherent tone. Avoid explaining every implication or ending with a universal lesson.

commitments.text: The umbrella contains no hidden message, treasure, weapon, or supernatural property.
The scene stays at the lost-property counter.

prompt: This is an invented teaching dossier, not real historical evidence. Write a short historical analysis explaining what changed at the fictional Northbank mill and how strongly the packet supports a causal explanation for the injury decline. Develop a clear argument, discuss rival mechanisms and measurement limits, and preserve the uncertainty in the evidence. Use only this packet.

sources.title: Northbank inspection ledger
sources.author: Municipal inspector
sources.perspective: Administrative annual summary; gives rates but not case-level records.
sources.text: In 1855 the Northbank mill recorded twelve injuries per thousand worker-days. New machine guards were installed in February 1856. The recorded injury rate in 1856 was seven per thousand worker-days.

sources.title: Northbank directors' report
sources.author: Mill directors
sources.text: During 1856 the working day was reduced from twelve hours to ten. Management attributed the fall in recorded injuries to its new guards. The report did not separately estimate the effects of shorter hours.

sources.title: Inspector's correspondence
sources.author: Municipal inspector
sources.perspective: Private administrative correspondence about data availability.
sources.text: No comparable injury series is available for the neighboring mill. The annual ledger does not report changes in the age or experience of the Northbank workforce. The reporting rules are described as unchanged.

prompt: This is an invented teaching dossier. Write an evidence-led account of a clash in the fictional town of Mereford. Distinguish what the sources agree on, what they dispute, and what cannot be established. Assess each source's opportunity to observe and interest in the outcome. Do not invent a neutral witness or decide the disputed sequence merely because one account sounds more vivid.

sources.title: Captain's report
sources.author: Captain of the town guard
sources.perspective: Official account submitted in defense of the guard's conduct.
sources.text: A crowd assembled outside the town hall. The captain reported that stones were thrown before mounted guards entered the square. He wrote that three guards were injured and that the assembly was then dispersed.

sources.title: Petition from assembly participants
sources.author: Six named assembly participants
sources.perspective: Petition requesting an inquiry; the signatories participated in the assembly.
sources.text: The petition agreed that the crowd assembled outside the town hall and was dispersed by the guard. It alleged that mounted guards entered before any stones were thrown. It listed five injured participants.

sources.title: Merchant's letter
sources.author: Merchant whose shop faced a side street
sources.perspective: Personal letter; limited view of the square.
sources.text: The merchant heard shouting and then looked out. He saw guards moving through the crowd but could not see the beginning of the confrontation. His letter did not count the injured.

prompt: This invented dossier concerns surviving records in a fictional district. Write a short historical explanation of whether the recorded decline demonstrates that fewer disputes occurred. Separate the observed counts from the process that produced the records. Address what a defensible conclusion can say and what further evidence would be needed, without inventing it.

sources.title: District annual docket
sources.author: District clerk
sources.text: The docket lists forty cases in 1800 and twenty-two cases in 1801. The surviving 1800 ledger covers the whole district. No monthly breakdown survives for either year.

sources.title: Clerk's note on jurisdiction
sources.author: District clerk
sources.perspective: Procedural explanation of the ledger's scope.
sources.text: From March 1801, disputes from the eastern parishes were entered in a separate book. That book is now missing. The surviving district ledger continued to record western-parish cases.

sources.title: Magistrate's retrospective memorandum
sources.author: Former district magistrate
sources.text: The former magistrate wrote that the district had become more orderly during his term. The memorandum provided no case counts, population estimates, or account of changes in jurisdiction.
